one_liner: Tracing JIT compiler and assembler-written interpreter for Lua 5.1; runs Lua code several times faster than PUC-Rio Lua 5.4.
what_it_does: LuaJIT is a complete Lua implementation (standalone `luajit` binary plus an embeddable library) that is API- and ABI-compatible with the Lua 5.1 C API, so an application that embeds Lua 5.1 usually only has to link against a different library. On top of Lua 5.1 it ships the `bit` module, an FFI that declares and calls C functions and C data structures directly from Lua, the `jit.*` control module, a profiler and selected Lua 5.2/5.3 extensions. Since 2026-07-20 the v2.1 branch also accepts some LuaJIT 3.0 syntax (native bit operators, `!=`, ternary, compound assignment, `continue`), but it is still not Lua 5.3/5.4.
how_it_is_fast: Two tiers: a fast bytecode interpreter written in assembler through DynASM, and a trace compiler that records hot loops and calls (hotloop default 56 iterations), turns them into SSA IR and optimizes them with constant folding, CSE, loop-invariant hoisting, load/store forwarding, array bounds check elimination, allocation sinking and operand fusion before emitting machine code. FFI cdata accesses (for example a `uint8_t[?]` or `bool[?]` array) are compiled to plain loads and stores, which is part of why the kostya/benchmarks `*_jit.lua` variants are fast.
when_to_use: Embedding a scripting language in a C or C++ application (games, network proxies such as OpenResty, appliances) where Lua 5.1 semantics are acceptable and script CPU time matters.
Numeric and loop-heavy Lua code: same-source kostya/jit-benchmarks numbers show about 10x to 30x over Lua 5.4.4 on nbody, mandelbrot, spectralnorm and matmul.
Code that needs to call C libraries or work on raw C arrays and structs from Lua without writing C binding code (FFI).
Platforms on the supported list: x86, x64, ARM, ARM64, PPC, MIPS32, MIPS64 on Windows, Linux, BSD, macOS, Android and consoles.
when_not_to_use: Code written for Lua 5.3/5.4: there is no integer subtype, no `//` floor division, no `_ENV`, no bit operator metamethods; 5.2 compatibility is partial and some parts need a -DLUAJIT_ENABLE_LUA52COMPAT build.
String-library and pattern-matching workloads: LuaJIT lost regexdna to Lua 5.4.4 in kostya/jit-benchmarks (9.99 s vs 8.94 s) and gained only 2.2x on fasta and 2.6x on revcomp.

Platforms that forbid runtime code generation (iOS, consoles): the JIT is disabled there and only the interpreter runs; the docs say it is still faster than plain Lua, but the large speedups disappear.
Untrusted scripts that get FFI access: the FFI has no memory safety (out-of-bounds array access or a misdeclared C function can crash the process).
Allocation-heavy workloads where memory is tight: binarytrees peaked at 307.5 MB under LuaJIT vs 145.2 MB under Lua 5.4.4.

integration.form: static lib | shared lib (libluajit / lua51.dll) plus standalone luajit executable
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C library (-lm -ldl on Linux when linking statically)
integration.min_toolchain: Recent GCC, Clang/LLVM or MSVC; GNU Make for the POSIX/MinGW build. The docs ask you to build it with its own build system and not to drop its sources into your tree. Default flags are -O2 -fomit-frame-pointer.
integration.platforms: x86, x64, ARM, ARM64, PPC, MIPS32, MIPS64; Windows, Linux, BSD, macOS, POSIX, Android, iOS (interpreter only), PS4/PS5/Xbox/Switch (interpreter only)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented beyond the Lua 5.1 model: separate lua_State instances are independent; one state must not be used from several threads at once.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: drop-in for Lua 5.1 (API+ABI compatible, including C modules); not a drop-in for the Lua 5.4.7 baseline used in the benchmark because 5.3/5.4 integer and operator semantics differ

gotchas: Harness flaw in the headline source: kostya/benchmarks runs different scripts under the two interpreters. bf_jit.lua is a different design from bf.lua (one closure per instruction, a fixed 8192-cell uint8_t FFI tape with no bounds check, separate inc/dec closures) while bf.lua uses a growing Lua table of unbounded integers and an if-chain dispatcher; primes_jit.lua swaps the Lua table for an FFI bool[] sieve. The 6.5x (bench.b) and 3.4x (primes) ratios therefore mix interpreter speed with data-structure choices. bench.b never underflows a cell, so the outputs agree.

In kostya's primes.lua (the plain-Lua baseline) fill_array writes a global `a` (missing `local`), adding a global lookup per element over 5,000,001 iterations; primes_jit.lua does not have this cost because it uses ffi.new. The handicap is small but it favours LuaJIT.

The kostya/benchmarks README version table is partly stale (it lists Java 24.0.2 and Go 1.25.0 while docker/Dockerfile installs JDK 26.0.1 and Go 1.26.5); its LuaJIT row 2.1.1748495995 carries a 2025-05-29 commit timestamp although the Dockerfile builds openresty/luajit2 v2.1-20260701, and it lists Lua 5.4.7 while the Dockerfile installs Debian lua5.5. Which binaries produced the timings is not certain.

Code the JIT cannot compile (NYI operations, for example some FFI operations such as table initializers, aggregates by value, ffi.cdef calls inside loops) silently falls back to the interpreter; check with `luajit -jv`. Use luaL_newstate, not lua_newstate with a custom allocator, and load the `jit` library, or the JIT stays off.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LuaJIT over LuaAOT (lua-aot-5.4), whose own README says it is not as fast as LuaJIT, and over Mobius, when your scripts can live with Lua 5.1 semantics; pick LuaAOT or stock Lua 5.4 when you need 5.4 integers and operators. Wren beat LuaJIT only with the JIT turned off (-joff) on its own method-call benchmark, so it is not a reason to skip LuaJIT for throughput.
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks (Xeon E-2324G, Docker on Debian forky, LuaJIT from openresty/luajit2 built with plain make, Lua from the Debian package) times LuaJIT at 5.686 s vs 37.051 s for Lua on bench.b and 0.309 s vs 1.056 s on primes, but with FFI-based *_jit.lua scripts on the LuaJIT side. The same-source kostya/jit-benchmarks round from 2023-02-28 (Ryzen 7 3800X, LuaJIT 2.1.0-beta3 vs Lua 5.4.4, both built with plain make, CPU time from os.clock) gives nbody 1.44 s vs 19.69 s and mandelbrot 0.5 s vs 5.39 s, but LuaJIT is slower on regexdna (9.99 s vs 8.94 s).
status_note: Actively maintained by Mike Pall on the rolling v2.1 branch (commits through 2026-09-08, including JIT fixes and the July 2026 syntax backport); MIT-licensed and copyable, with the GitHub repo a mirror of the official git repository and releases only as source or rolling 2.1.<timestamp> versions.
